newsitem.title: USA: Florida should divest tobacco stocks - atty general.
newsitem.headline: Florida should divest tobacco stocks - atty general.

text.p: Florida's attorney general on Tuesday said officials overseeing the state's $60 billion pension fund should dump almost $800 million in tobacco company stock when they meet to vote on the issue Wednesday.

"The possibility of future litigation, coupled with the potential for catastrophic losses, should prompt trustees overseeing the state's retirement portfolio to jettison the stock at the earliest possible instance," Attorney General Bob Butterworth said in an opinion released Tuesday.
Specifically, Butterworth was responding to a request of the Florida Division of Administration, which handles the pension fund for about 725,000 current and retired state employees.
The agency had asked for a legal opinion on whether it could divest traditionally high-performing tobacco stocks without violating its responsibility to maintain the pension fund prudently.
In a 12-page opinion, Butterworth said the agency could legally divest if a majority of the trustees vote Wednesday to do so.

"The test is not how much money it's going to make in the future," Butterworth said Tuesday. "The test is whether you used good faith and made a reasonable decision that a prudent person would make. These stocks have not been performing as well as other stock have been over the past couple years."

Butterworth has been a leading opponent of the tobacco industry and is presently involved in negotiations with company representatives over a possible nationwide settlement of tobacco-related litigation.

Last year, Gov. Lawton Chiles asked the state's pension administration to look at the ramifications of divesting Florida's tobacco portfolio. In September, the pension fund advisory board was deadlocked over whether the state should divest.
Chiles has publicly stated he favors divestiture, especially since the state is suing the tobacco industry for more than $1 billion in a civil lawsuit set to begin in West Palm Beach in August.

The state is suing the industry to recover costs paid into the Medicaid system for smoking-related illnesses. Though the advisory board failed to reach consensus, financial managers called in to assist said that the state should keep its tobacco holdings despite the increasing threat of litigation.
Florida's pension fund is overseen by a trio of state officials who act as trustees. They include Chiles, state Insurance Commissioner Bill Nelson and state Comptroller Bob Milligan.

Milligan has publicly stated he favors holding on to the stocks, saying that their historically high returns are all the investment board should be concerned about. Nelson has not publicly stated his position. An ardent anti-smoker, Nelson has nonetheless kept his vote a secret.
